headline: Peconic settles into deep summer — porgies thick at Shelter Island, bass gone to the night shift
subhead: The bay's locked into its July rhythm: daytime belongs to porgies and fluke in the channels, nighttime belongs to stripers working the rips.
body_markdown:
The Peconic runs on its own clock, and by late July that clock says: warm water up top, cooler water down deep, and fish sorting themselves accordingly. This bay always warms ahead of the Sound and the ocean beaches — it's shallow, it's protected, and the sun's had all spring and half the summer to work on it. Right now it's sitting warm and glassy on most mornings, especially up in Noyack Bay and the upper reaches of Three Mile Harbor, and that heat is doing exactly what it does this time of year: pushing the day-biters into structure and sending the stripers to work the night shift.

We flagged this pattern last week — said conditions would hold stable through the stretch, no major disruption — and that's precisely what's played out. No storms, no cold fronts, no big wind events to stir things up. Just steady heat and a bay settling into its mid-summer groove.

Start with the good news, because there's real good news: porgy fishing around Shelter Island is as good as it gets anywhere on the East Coast right now. The west side drop-offs off Cedar Island and the deeper water outside Coecles Harbor are holding heavy, hungry schools in that 15- to 25-foot range. Standard hi-lo rig, size 6 or 4 hooks, sandworm or skimmer clam, dropped right to bottom on the last of the incoming or the first hour of the outgoing when the current's still got some push but hasn't gone slack. You don't need to finesse these fish — they're stacked and they're eating. The trick this week has been sizing up your bait a little, because the small stuff gets picked clean by the shorts before a keeper-class porgy even gets a shot. Bigger clam chunks are weeding out some of that nuisance bite and putting bigger fish in the cooler.

Fluke have done what fluke do in a warm July — they've pulled off the open flats and tucked into the channels where the water keeps moving and stays a few degrees cooler. The bend in the Noyack Bay channel and the deeper cuts near the Three Mile Harbor entrance have both been holding fish, though I won't call it easy. It's been a numbers game more than a slam-dunk — you're covering water, working bucktail-and-Gulp combinations (white or chartreuse, 3/4-ounce head, 5-inch Gulp Swimming Mullet trailer) on a slow drift through 20 to 35 feet, and you're culling through a fair number of shorts to find the keepers. Best window has been the last two hours of the outgoing, when the current is still moving enough to keep that Gulp trailer working but hasn't gone dead calm and lifeless. A couple of guys have done well switching to bigger, fresh-cut squid strips on the same rig when the current slows — bigger profile seems to trigger fewer but better-quality bites in that stagnant water.

Weakfish are still around if you know where to look, and the deeper holes in Gardiners Bay have been the most consistent producer — that's a dusk-into-dark bite, working bucktails tipped with squid or drifting a bunker chunk on a fish-finder rig right along the bottom where the deeper, cooler water holds. It's not a numbers fishery the way it was a generation ago, but the ones that come over the rail have been quality fish, and the evening bite has been the reliable window.

Striped bass have gone quiet during daylight, which tracks with what's happening up and down the whole coast this time of year — surface water in the low-to-mid 70s pushes them down onto structure and current edges, and they mostly stay there until dark. The move is fishing the rips at night: Plum Gut, the drop-offs off Orient Point, and the current seams along the edges of Shelter Island's east side. Eels fished on a fish-finder rig or bunker chunks soaked on the bottom have been the producers, and the bite windows are tight — usually tied right to the tide change, whether that's the top of the flood or the start of the outgoing. The moon's building toward full over the next week or so, and that means the current through Plum Gut and the Race is going to sharpen up considerably. That's worth watching closely, because a stronger push through that gut usually means a better window for bigger bass working the rip edges after dark.

Bluefish have been showing in that classic sporadic, opportunistic way — chasing bait right into the inlets and creek mouths, especially around Sag Harbor and the mouth of Three Mile Harbor. Nothing sustained, but when a school of bait gets pinned up against structure on a moving tide, the blues show up fast and leave just as quick. Worth keeping a metal or a popper rigged and ready if you're working those areas, because you won't get much warning.

One thing worth watching as we roll into August: with the heat this settled and the wind this calm, the shallow, mud-bottom stretches of the upper bay — parts of Noyack, the back ends of the harbors — can start to run low on oxygen if nothing stirs the water for stretches at a time. I haven't seen distress yet, but it's the kind of thing that sneaks up on a bay like this. If you're fishing those upper reaches, the early morning and late evening hours are going to fish better than midday, both for comfort and because that's when the water's freshest.

Bay scallop prep is underway too — a few boats have been out checking grass beds ahead of the fall opener, and the early read is encouraging, though it's early. If the current pattern holds — stable heat, building moon current, porgies stacked at Shelter Island — I'd expect more of the same through early August: good daytime action on porgies and fluke, a quality-over-quantity weakfish bite at dusk, and stripers staying loyal to the night shift until something finally breaks the heat.
